applicability.notes: N001 is instantiated on the one-dimensional Euclidean set I, with a>1 for the zero-measure implication and 0<s<1 for the infinite-measure implication; both exponents are positive. The interval-length and countable-subadditivity facts apply to measurable bounded open J_i, without requiring the original V_i to be measurable. argument.notes: For each fixed scale, the N equal intervals are eventually admissible and their a-cost tends to zero, so every scale content and hence H^a(I) vanish. The enlarged intervals give 1≤Σρ_i+ε for every ε>0, yielding Σρ_i≥1 including the infinite-sum case. The pointwise power inequality includes ρ_i=0, and its nonnegative sum gives the stated lower bound for every cover and then its infimum. Taking the supremum over positive scales gives infinite H^s(I); no interchange of limits, infima or sums is required. N001 and the endpoint order arguments give dimension exactly one.

statement_closure.notes: The packet specifies the Euclidean metric, unnormalized scale contents and measures, dimension convention, I=[0,1], and Lebesgue measure. Countable covers are handled as subsets of the real line with nonempty members indexed by K⊆ℕ. The output supplies the exact dimension equality, every a>1 zero-measure clause, and every 0<s<1, δ>0 lower bound and infinite-measure clause. All are proved with those domains and normalization; unused ambient n,E impose no condition.

background_notes.fact: If V⊆ℝ is nonempty and diam(V)=ρ≤δ<∞, then V is bounded, α=inf V and β=sup V are finite real numbers, β−α=ρ, and for every η>0, V⊆(α−η,β+η).

grounds.reason: L3 gives δ>0; L4 gives nonempty V_i with finite diameters ρ_i≤δ.
Diameter is the supremum of Euclidean pairwise distances.

background_notes.justification: Choose v∈V. Every x∈V satisfies |x−v|≤δ, giving upper and lower bounds and hence real infimum and supremum. Every pairwise distance is at most β−α. Conversely, points of V can approach α from above and β from below, so their distances approach β−α; thus the diameter equals this difference. The infimum/supremum inequalities give the stated open-interval containment.

background_notes.fact: Lebesgue measure satisfies λ([0,1])=1, λ((u,v))=v−u for finite real u<v, and λ(B)≤Σ_i λ(B_i) whenever a measurable B is covered by a countable family of measurable B_i.

grounds.reason: λ is Lebesgue measure and sums are nonnegative extended sums.
I is the measurable closed interval [0,1].
ε>0 and finite endpoints ensure that every J_i is a bounded open interval; these intervals cover I.

background_notes.justification: Lebesgue interval normalization gives the two length formulas; interval endpoints have measure zero, so the closed interval has the same length. For the covering inequality, replace each B_i by its part outside earlier B_j; these measurable parts are disjoint, have no larger measures, and have the same union. Countable additivity and monotonicity then give the inequality. This uses no measurability of V_i.

background_notes.fact: For K⊆ℕ, Σ_{i∈K}2^(−i−1)≤1. Consequently, for nonnegative real ρ_i and ε>0, Σ_{i∈K}(ρ_i+ε2^(−i−1))≤Σ_{i∈K}ρ_i+ε. If a fixed S∈[0,∞] satisfies 1≤S+ε for every ε>0, then S≥1.

grounds.reason: K⊆ℕ, ρ_i≥0 and ε>0 are fixed there; the sum S=Σρ_i is independent of ε.
Nonnegative sums are suprema of finite partial sums.

background_notes.justification: The first M terms of the full geometric series sum to 1−2^(−M), tending to 1; subseries cannot increase a nonnegative sum. Addition and finite nonnegative scalar multiplication commute with these increasing finite sums, including an infinite value. For the last assertion the infinite case is immediate; if finite S<1, choosing ε=(1−S)/2 contradicts 1≤S+ε.

background_notes.fact: For countably many nonnegative b_i,c_i and finite C>0, b_i≥C c_i for every i implies Σ_i b_i≥C Σ_i c_i, also when Σ_i c_i=∞.

grounds.reason: Here b_i=ρ_i^s, c_i=ρ_i, C=δ^(s−1)>0, and the pointwise inequality is proved separately for positive and zero ρ_i.
The sums have nonnegative extended values.

background_notes.justification: Sum the inequalities over each finite set of indices and take suprema. Multiplication by a positive finite constant preserves these suprema; if the sum of c_i is infinite, its finite sums exceed any prescribed finite bound, and so do the scaled sums.

background_notes.fact: For positive real x and real r, x^r=exp(r log x); real powers obey x^s=x·x^(s−1) and 0^s=0 for s>0. If r<0 and 0<x≤y, then x^r≥y^r. For p>0, N^(−p)→0 as positive integers N→∞, and δ^(−p)→∞ as δ↓0.

grounds.reason: a>1 and N≥1 give p=a−1>0 and cost N^(−p); 1/N also tends to zero for scale admissibility.
0<s<1 and 0<ρ_i≤δ give r=s−1<0; zero diameters are treated using s>0.
For fixed 0<s<1, p=1−s>0 and δ ranges over every positive scale.

background_notes.justification: The exponential representation gives the exponent identity and reverses monotonicity when the exponent is negative. The logarithm tends to infinity at infinity and to minus infinity at zero, while exp tends to infinity and to zero at the corresponding ends. Applying these facts with p>0 proves the two power limits. Thus vanishing costs apply at each fixed positive scale, and the lower bounds δ^(s−1) exceed every finite number at sufficiently small scales.
